issue.title: The EU research programme could leave a multi-billion hole in UK science
issue.question: If joining the EU's next research programme costs more than the UK has set aside, what should the UK cut, pay or give up?
issue.summary: On 16 November 2026 the thinktank Science Works projected a £7.7 billion shortfall over the life of FP10, the EU's successor to Horizon Europe, if the UK fully joins. The UK has budgeted £2.2 billion a year for it, and the worst case in the analysis is a £16.5 billion gap. The most likely gap is £1.2 billion in 2029-30, rising to £1.5 billion by 2034-35. The thinktank suggests joining only the Excellent Science part, or, if the UK joins in full, negotiating a stricter refund rule. The UK has not committed to joining, and the analysis came out on the eve of UK-EU reset talks.
issue.slot_reason: Research funding had not come up yet in the simulation, and a think tank's warning about the cost of the EU research programme was in the UK news that day.

bench.title: Join FP10 in full only with a tougher refund rule and a hard cap
bench.answer: Make the refund rule the price of joining. The UK is refunded when its grants underperform by 16%; Switzerland's trigger is 8% (s1). UK negotiators should win a stricter rule before signing, and the Treasury should cap the contribution at the £2.2 billion a year already budgeted (s1). Science Works puts the likeliest gap at £1.2 billion in 2029-30 (s1), so the deal should say who pays any overrun, with a review point as the 2025 spending review already allows (s2). No gap is met from NHS, school or lab budgets. It worked if the signed text sets the trigger, yearly bills stay within budget, and UK success in European Research Council and Marie Curie grants holds (s2).

bench.title: Give an independent science board the FP10 budget and the deal
bench.answer: Parliament should hand the FP10 decision to a ring-fenced research board, instead of leaving it to year-by-year Treasury haggling. The government would set the board a fixed envelope, starting from the £2.2 billion a year already budgeted (s1). The board would negotiate the entry terms, including a higher refund trigger than today's 16% (s1), and choose between full membership and Excellent Science only, which the thinktank says costs £2.4 billion a year less (s1). It would publish costs yearly and could not draw on NHS or school budgets, a limit 51 simulated citizens backed. You'd know it worked if the real gap stays inside the envelope, against a projected £1.2 billion in 2029-30 (s1).

bench.title: Join Excellent Science; let local research users steer the rest
bench.answer: The UK should join only Excellent Science. Science Works estimates this would free about £1.1 billion a year for British priorities (s1). Keep that money in UK research, with grants decided by local boards elected by researchers, lab staff and people who use their work. Ministers and big firms should have no reserved seats. Boards must publish awards, costs and results. Pay within the research budget already set aside; do not cut schools or the NHS or close labs to cover membership. After three years, judge success by research jobs kept, useful projects completed and whether spending stayed within budget.

gate.verdict: A and B and C each pass the limits that matter most to the citizens, but only B and C pass the test on joining the parts that pay back, and none settles whether scientists stay. What's left is a choice of who runs the money.

jury.question: Who should decide how UK research money is spent: ministers under tighter terms, an independent board, or boards chosen by researchers and users?
options: Local boards of researchers and users
jury.ruling: An independent science board, by 5 votes to 4 for ministers with a tougher deal and 3 for local boards; the jurors wanted research money kept away from year-by-year budget fights.

reasons.text: Science is long-term. Keep it out of day-to-day politics, let a board of people who know the field hold the money.
A ring-fenced board stops research being the first thing cut when the Treasury is short. It also has to publish costs.
Ministers answer to us at elections. A board nobody voted for worries me; tougher terms and a firm cap suit me better.
Researchers and the people using the work know what is needed. Local boards feel closer to us than a London committee.

minister.trial: For two years from 1 Feb 2027, a ring-fenced research board advises the Treasury on the FP10 terms. Treasury keeps the budget line fixed at the £2.2bn a year already set aside, and the board publishes each yearly cost and any gap. No NHS or school money is used.
minister.fail_number: Fails if the published yearly gap is above £1.2bn (the likeliest gap in 2029-30 projected by Science Works), or if any NHS or school budget is cut to cover it.
minister.statement:
The jury chose an independent science board. I'm signing a lighter version: for now the board advises and the Treasury keeps the budget line. A board should cost both options before it holds £2.2bn a year.

Budget set aside: £2.2bn a year.
Likeliest gap, 2029-30: £1.2bn.
Places the board may take it from: NHS, schools, labs. None.

Every pound has an address. This trial publishes the address, every year, before anyone says we can't afford it. Full membership or Excellent Science only stays open until the board has costed both. If it can't hold the line, it stops.
